section_1.title: The Hook: The Constant Ratio
section_1.content: Introduce the fundamental observation: regardless of size, every circle maintains a constant relationship between its circumference (C) and diameter (d). Explain this as a ratio C/d.
section_1.example: An animated hamster wheel vs. a giant Ferris wheel; both share the same magical ratio hidden in their dimensions.

section_2.title: Defining Pi (π)
section_2.content: Formalize the definition: π is the mathematical constant representing the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. Note that it is an irrational number (infinite, non-repeating).
section_2.example: Visualizing a 'unrolling' process: stretch the circumference of a circle into a straight line and see that it is exactly 3.14 times the length of the diameter.

section_3.title: Historical Evolution: The Polygon Method
section_3.content: Explain Archimedes' 'Method of Exhaustion.' Before modern calculus, mathematicians approximated π by inscribing and circumscribing polygons with increasing numbers of sides around a circle.
section_3.example: An animation showing a triangle inside a circle transforming into a square, a pentagon, and eventually a 96-sided polygon, getting closer and closer to the circle's boundary.

section_4.title: Modern Applications and Computation
section_4.content: Transition from geometry to modern utility. Pi is essential in engineering, space travel, and computer science for random number generation and signal processing.
section_4.example: A robot arm drawing a perfectly smooth circle using the formula C = πd; showing how precise Pi is needed to ensure the arm doesn't jitter or gap.

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap: π is not just a number, but a bridge between linear and circular geometry. Encourage students to view it as a universal constant present in nature and technology.
section_5.example: A quick visual montage: a slice of pie, a circular planet orbit, and a digital watch, all connected by the symbol π.
